articles.title: US clears $2.1 billion Patriot missile deal for Ukraine, with Europe and Canada footing bill
articles.summary: The US state department on Friday approved a possible sale of 500 Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) interceptors to
articles.body: The US state department on Friday approved a possible sale of 500 Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) interceptors to Ukraine, in a deal estimated to be worth $2.1 billion and funded entirely by Kyiv's partners and allies.Ukraine has been facing shortages of US-made Patriot air defence systems and PAC-3 interceptors, which can be used to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. Intensified Russian attacks over the past two months have forced people across the country to increasingly seek shelter, with air raid alerts becoming part of daily life.However, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed the move, he also urged Washington to facilitate faster deliveries, saying the missiles are needed to counter Russian attacks during the coming winter.“Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package. However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelenskyy said.“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” he added.According to the US state department's notification, Ukraine has requested to purchase 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles, along with classified and unclassified spare parts and other related logistics and programme support.The purchase would be funded through donations from Canada, Germany and Norway via the Jumpstart programme, as well as national funds financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan.“No U.S. funds are involved in this sale,” the notification said.The principal contractor for the proposed sale is Lockheed Martin.According to the state department, the proposed sale would improve Ukraine's ability to respond to current and future threats by strengthening its integrated air and missile defence capabilities. It would also sustain the operation of existing Patriot systems against ongoing aerial threats.Zelenskyy seeks immediate supply of interceptorsWhile welcoming the authorisation, Zelenskyy said Ukraine needed the interceptors during the winter of 2026-2027 rather than several years later.He said Russia had continued targeting Ukraine's energy infrastructure, with more than 30 strikes on critical parts of the country's power grid during the first two weeks of October alone.“Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day,” Zelenskyy said, adding that Russian attacks were targeting electricity, heating, water supplies and bridges, as well as life in Ukrainian cities and communities.The Ukrainian president said Kyiv had asked its American partners for a winter support package involving 100 Patriot interceptors a month.Zelenskyy proposed that the US and its partners supply Ukraine with interceptors from their existing stocks during the winter, and replenish their arsenals in subsequent years through production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and its partners.“The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses,” he said, adding that supplying them immediately and replenishing the stocks later would be “entirely feasible”.Previously, the US secretary of state Marco Rubio described the interceptors as the as the “most in-demand product” in the defence sector.“When a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying. We have our own. We have minimum standards that we have to meet internally in our base presence all over the world,” Rubio said.He added that the US maintained a global defence footprint, with many of its installations around the world relying on air defence systems.“So there's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” Rubio said.On Friday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine's long-range strike capabilities were an important element of its security.“Ukraine's long-range strike capabilities are one of the real guarantees of our independence now, during this war, and they will remain one of our long-term security guarantees after it ends,” he said in an X post.

articles.summary: JAIPUR: The Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) Friday registered a preliminary inquiry against senior IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal for allegedly misusing his
articles.body: JAIPUR: The Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) Friday registered a preliminary inquiry against senior IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal for allegedly misusing his official position to favour a private company and causing financial losses to the state govt.The state govt formally approved of an investigation against Agrawal earlier in the day. He was serving as an additional chief secretary, industries, when he was put on awaiting posting orders (APO) status Wednesday.At the centre of the probe are alleged irregularities in the purchase of villas by Agrawal and family members.The bureau, in a statement, alleged that Agrawal colluded with the directors of Goyal Fashions Private Limited, which operates hotels and resorts under the brand name ‘Ananta’, to secure undue benefits for the company.These allegedly included relaxations in conditions governing resort construction, approvals without verification of mandatory certificates and a special concessional financial package.The bureau said preliminary investigations also found that Agrawal colluded with the company’s directors to buy villas at its Ananta resorts in his own name and those of his family members. In March 2026, he allegedly purchased 20 villas at the company’s Bujhda resort in Udaipur, besides acquiring villas at its resort at Ajabgarh in Alwar district.Eight Ajabgarh villas bought for 16.5L eachAccording to information gathered during preliminary investigations, Sikhar Agrawal and his IPS officer wife Prashakha Mathur purchased 10 villas each at the Bujhda resort in Udaipur for Rs 15 lakh apiece. At the Ajabgarh resort in Alwar, eight villas were purchased in their names for Rs 16.5 lakh each.Their two sons acquired four villas at approximately Rs 15 lakh each, and an additional four were acquired in the name of other relatives for approximately Rs 16.5 lakh each.The bureau suspects that the family acquired these properties at prices substantially below market value.“Confidential sources have also revealed that Agrawal registered the purchase of 20 villas on March 27 this year, the same day the Finance Department issued a special concessional financial package to Goyal Fashions Private Limited,” the bureau claimed.It alleged that Agrawal colluded with the company’s directors during his tenure in govt, helping the company secure undue benefits and causing substantial financial losses to the state.ACB said it also found it necessary to investigate whether he had accumulated assets disproportionate to his known sources of income in his own name and those of his family members. The agency said it had perused newspaper reports, examined a factual report from the industries department and gathered information from confidential sources before registering the inquiry against Agrawal.The bureau said preliminary investigations also found that Agrawal colluded with the company’s directors to buy villas at its Ananta resorts in his own name and those of his family members.ACB said it was also examining alleged misuse by Agrawal of his official position during past tenures as Udaipur district collector, chairperson of the Rajasthan State Pollution Control Board and additional chief secretary, Industries, among others.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Jaipur | Silver Rate in Jaipur | Bank Holidays in Jaipur | Public Holidays in Jaipur | Jaipur AQI | Weather in Jaipur | Petrol Price in Jaipur | Diesel Price in Jaipur | CNG Price in Jaipur | LPG Price in JaipurStay updated with the latest Jaipur news. articles.title: 11-year-old Egyptian girl beats 40 million students in reading contest; what Dubai ruler Sheikh Mohammed did after her win caught attention
articles.summary: An emotional victory, a Dh500,000 prize and an unexpected gesture from one of the world's most powerful leaders made 11-year-old Mayar Othman Al
articles.body: An emotional victory, a Dh500,000 prize and an unexpected gesture from one of the world's most powerful leaders made 11-year-old Mayar Othman Al Shourbagy's moment in Dubai unforgettable. After she was crowned the winner of the 10th Arab Reading Challenge, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum removed the badge he was wearing and pinned it onto the young Egyptian student. Mayar had just achieved something remarkable. She emerged as the champion of the 10th edition of the Arab Reading Challenge, beating more than 40 million students from 60 countries. And as she stood before Sheikh Mohammed, Vice President and Prime Minister of the UAE and Ruler of Dubai, he did something that went beyond presenting her with a trophy.According to a report by Gulf News, Sheikh Mohammed kissed Mayar on the head, held her close affectionately and then removed his own badge to pin it onto her. Why did Sheikh Mohammed give Mayar his own badge?While Sheikh Mohammed did not publicly explain the specific reason behind the gesture, it appeared to be a personal expression of appreciation and encouragement for the young champion. The badge was not part of the announced competition prize. Rather, it was a personal gesture from the Dubai ruler as he congratulated the young student on her achievement.When Mayar’s name was announced as the winner, she jumped up in joy, knelt down and kissed the floor in gratitude before breaking down in tears.This was also not the first time Sheikh Mohammed had gifted his badge to a young student. During a visit to Al Ibda'a Model School in Dubai, he had removed his badge and pinned it onto six-year-old Rayyan Badr Mohammed after the boy confidently recited the ruler's full name, as per Gulf News. That badge was a special-edition Expo 2020 Dubai keepsake.Who is Mayar Othman Al Shourbagy, the girl who beat 40 million students?Mayar's victory was the result of a reading journey that began at school. The 11-year-old Egyptian student read 60 books during her preparation for the competition and was selected from among 17,616,289 contestants in Egypt. “My journey began at school, when my supervisor noticed that I could speak Arabic confidently and had an enlightened outlook,” Mayar said according to Gulf News. She initially started reading poetry before moving on to books, summarising them with what she described as wisdom, intelligence and precision. “My mother, father and entire family supported me. My school also provided the right environment that enabled me to win this title,” she said. Her achievement earned her the championship title and a cash prize of Dh500,000.A competition that brought together over 40 million studentsThe 10th Arab Reading Challenge attracted 40,286,428 students from 60 countries, representing 138,426 schools and 161,507 supervisors. The initiative, launched by Sheikh Mohammed in 2015, aims to encourage reading, strengthen Arabic language skills and nurture a love for knowledge among younger generations.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'My body hurts, my soul hurts': Christa Pike's first statement after failed execution in US
articles.summary: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has said she remains in constant physical and psychological pain after surviving a botched lethal injection on
articles.body: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has said she remains in constant physical and psychological pain after surviving a botched lethal injection on September 30. In her first public statement since the failed execution, the 50-year-old described her injuries, isolation in a prison hospital and uncertainty about her future.In a statement dictated to her lawyers and released on Friday, the 50-year-old said she had been struggling with pain and speech difficulties since the execution attempt.“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak,” Pike said.“And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.”Pike, who is being held at the Debra K Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Tennessee, said she had prepared herself to die peacefully but instead regained consciousness alone in a hospital bed.“I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next,” she said, adding that she was “searching for meaning in what happened to me”.She also expressed concern for the family of her victim, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.“I continue to think about my victim’s family,” Pike said, referring to the “terrible pain and loss they have endured”.Pike thanked the first responders and medical staff who treated her, saying support from people around the world had given her strength.“To know that so many people care about me, that they see me as a human being whose life matters, is something I cannot fully put into words,” she said.Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital during her scheduled execution at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution on September 30. Her lawyers said the injections may not have entered her bloodstream correctly, instead pooling in her arms and causing severe injuries, including burns and blistering.According to court documents, the execution team struggled to establish functioning intravenous lines. Pike reportedly complained of burning pain before losing consciousness and being transferred to a Nashville hospital in critical condition. She was discharged on October 10.Her lawyers have also asked a federal judge to end her isolation in the prison infirmary, arguing that it violates a 2024 agreement allowing her social contact with other women prisoners. They said the isolation had caused significant psychological harm.Meanwhile, a Tennessee judge has ordered officials to preserve evidence relating to the failed execution. Her lawyers have alleged that the incident violated the constitutional prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment.Governor Bill Lee has appointed a former US attorney to review the incident and suspended the state's remaining executions for the year. The move follows another problematic execution attempt in May.Lee rejected Pike's clemency appeal before the execution attempt. Asked about her sentence this week, he said, “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”Pike remains on death row. Her lawyers are seeking to have her sentence commuted to life imprisonment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Canada's immigration authority to international students: You can only work in Canada if your study permit conditions says …
articles.summary: Canada's immigration authority has issued a fresh reminder to international students, warning that they can work in the country only if their study permit
articles.body: Canada's immigration authority has issued a fresh reminder to international students, warning that they can work in the country only if their study permit explicitly allows it and that violating work conditions could have serious consequences, including the loss of student status and possible removal from Canada. In a recent post, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) highlighted key rules that international students must follow while working during their studies. The agency said students can only work in Canada if the conditions listed on their study permit authorize them to work on or off campus. “Important information for international students who plan to work while studying:• You can only work in Canada as an international student if your study permit conditions say you can.• If you are eligible to work off campus, you can only work up to 24 hours per week while classes are in session.• Working more than you are allowed is a violation of your study permit conditions, which can have serious consequences,” wrote IRCC in a post on X (formerly known as Twitter).What the rules sayIRCC’s guidance says a student can work on or off campus only if the study permit lists a condition allowing it. The department tells students to pay close attention to the number of hours they are allowed to work off campus. A study permit is the document that sets out these terms, and holding one does not give automatic permission to take a job.Study permit must allow workThe immigration department stated that international students are eligible to work in Canada only if their study permit contains a condition permitting on-campus or off-campus employment. Students have been advised to carefully review their permits before accepting any job. IRCC's social media post also reminded students that those eligible to work off campus can work a maximum of 24 hours per week while classes are in session. Working beyond the permitted limit constitutes a violation of study permit conditions.Risk of losing student statusAccording to the agency, students who work more hours than allowed risk losing their student status. The department noted that non-compliance with permit conditions could also affect future applications for study permits or work permits. In some cases, individuals may be required to leave Canada. "Working more hours than you're allowed is a violation of your study permit conditions," IRCC said, adding that students could face consequences if they fail to follow the employment rules attached to their permits.Consequences of working too many hoursAccording to IRCC’s page on unauthorized work, working more than the allowed hours breaches the study permit conditions. A student who does so can lose their student status, and future study or work permit applications may be refused. The student may also have to leave the country.The department’s wider warning about unauthorized work, which applies to anyone working in Canada without permission, lists further risks. These include removal from Canada, a permanent record of fraud with IRCC and a five-year ban on returning. Such a record can also hurt the chances of future applications being approved, including for permanent residence. IRCC also says people working without authorisation face greater risks of unsafe conditions, wage theft, abuse and forced or unpaid labour.Working after graduationIRCC says students who want to work after they graduate generally need a work permit, and some are eligible for a post-graduation work permit (PGWP). A graduate who has applied for a PGWP can work full-time while waiting for a decision, but only if certain conditions are met. The applicant must have held a valid study permit when applying, must have completed the program and must have been eligible to work off campus while studying without exceeding the allowed hours. Those who don’t meet these conditions must wait for their work permit before starting a new job.Watch for scamsIRCC’s guidance for workers also lists warning signs of immigration fraud, which students may encounter when looking for jobs. These include anyone who promises a work permit or job offer in exchange for payment, asks for documents or payment through social media, or offers free room and board in return for work. IRCC says people who work legally are protected by Canada’s labour laws and can contact provincial or territorial labour standards offices without their employer’s permission.You use AI every day. articles.title: A charity finance employee redirected a £91,966 payment meant for a breast cancer organisation into his own account and spent £14,000 on a ring for his wedding
articles.summary: A former charity finance employee in the UK has been sentenced to two years and six months in prison after diverting a £91,966 payment intended for a
articles.body: A former charity finance employee in the UK has been sentenced to two years and six months in prison after diverting a £91,966 payment intended for a breast cancer organisation into his personal bank account. Tameem Choudhury, 29, formerly employed by Breast Cancer Now, redirected the money by sending altered banking details to The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust, which was due to refund the charity. He later spent the money on personal debts, wedding and honeymoon expenses, luxury purchases and travel, including buying a £14,000 Alexander Brown ring. Choudhury was sentenced at the Royal Courts of Justice on September 1, 2026, after pleading guilty to fraud and money laundering offences. The charity confirmed that the funds were recovered and it suffered no financial loss.How the £91,966 payment was divertedAccording to the City of London Police, Breast Cancer Now was due to receive a refund of £91,966.72 from The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust in 2023. On August 11, 2023, Choudhury used his work email account to send altered bank details to the trust on letterhead bearing the charity's name. The account details provided belonged to him.The payment was transferred into his personal Santander account on August 16, 2024. The police report identifies the original instruction in 2023 and the eventual transfer in 2024.He spent £14,000 on a ring and funded wedding expensesInvestigators found that Choudhury used the money for a range of personal expenses, including paying off debts, making cash withdrawals, buying luxury items, paying for travel and transferring money to relatives.One of the purchases was an Alexander Brown ring worth £14,000. He also used the funds for wedding and honeymoon expenses, while airline tickets linked to travel to Qatar were among the spending identified during the investigation.Over just two days in September 2024, Choudhury spent £49,100.47 of the money, police said.Messages showed he was struggling with debtThe investigation uncovered evidence that Choudhury had been heavily in debt before receiving the payment. Messages recovered from his mobile phone showed him describing himself as “borderline broke” shortly before accessing the funds.Investigators traced spending to debt collection agencies, luxury retailers, travel expenses and transfers to family members. The findings formed part of the case against him for fraud and money laundering.How the fraud was uncoveredAfter suspicious activity was detected, Santander froze and subsequently closed Choudhury's account. At the time it was frozen, £42,866.25 remained in the account and was later recovered.Breast Cancer Now reported the matter to police, prompting an investigation by the City of London Police. Choudhury was arrested in June 2025. He later pleaded guilty to fraud and money laundering offences and was sentenced on September 1, 2026, to two years and six months in prison at the Royal Courts of Justice.Breast Cancer Now says funds were recoveredBreast Cancer Now said it had fully co-operated with the police investigation and reviewed its internal processes to reduce the risk of a similar incident occurring again.The charity also confirmed that the money had been recovered and that it had not suffered any financial loss. It said its work supporting people affected by breast cancer and funding research remained central to its mission.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: "I went through a lot of pain.." Her father had a dream for her at 59, Howrah’s Dolly Rana became a conductor to save the bus she bought to fulfil her late father’s dream
articles.summary: At 59, when many people might be thinking about slowing down, Dolly Rana is doing the opposite.
articles.body: At 59, when many people might be thinking about slowing down, Dolly Rana is doing the opposite. Every morning in Howrah, West Bengal, she steps onto a bus, ticket bag slung over her shoulder, and calls out stops to passengers. But for Rana, this is not simply a job. It is a promise she made to her father. Her journey is a reminder that some dreams never fade, even when life takes unexpected turns and years go by.A daughter’s journey to fulfil her father’s dreamRana’s father had always wanted to own a bus and enter the transport business. After his death, she decided to turn that long-held family dream into reality. In 2017, she took loans and bought a bus of her own. Initially, she hired a driver and conductor and managed the business herself. It was a significant financial commitment, but one she was willing to take for the dream her father had left behind.Then came the pandemic. Like much of the transport sector, Rana’s business was badly affected. When her conductor eventually quit in 2021 and losses continued to mount, she faced a choice: step away from the business or find another way to keep it going. She chose the latter.At 54, she stepped onto the bus herselfRana decided to become the conductor herself. There was no elaborate preparation. She simply got on duty and began learning the job as she went. In the beginning, she did not even have a conductor’s bag and collected passengers’ fares in the fold of her sari, she told The Telegraph. The work meant spending long hours on a crowded bus, jumping on and off repeatedly, issuing tickets, dealing with passengers and stepping in when disputes broke out. And she did it in a profession still overwhelmingly associated with men.Rana has said that being a woman in the job is difficult because some people continue to assume that women are weak. Passengers have questioned her and, at times, she has faced harassment. But she has continued to show up every morning. Her route, reported as bus number 57, runs between Belgachia and Howrah. Regular passengers have come to know her simply as “Dolly-di”.The bus became both her livelihood and her burdenOwning a bus brought its own set of problems. Maintenance costs rose, repairs became increasingly expensive and loan repayments added to the pressure. At the same time, the rise of electric rickshaws affected passenger numbers on parts of her route, cutting into her earnings. For Rana, however, giving up the bus would have meant giving up more than a source of income. It would have meant walking away from the dream that had motivated her in the first place. She eventually sought a new route permit that could help make the business viable again.One viral story led to a crucial phone callHer struggles gained wider attention after The Better India first shared her story and video. The attention eventually reached the state transport administration. According to The Better India, the state bus secretary personally contacted Rana and told her that her request for a new route permit had been approved. The new route offered her a better chance of continuing the business without facing the same level of competition from e-rickshaws. The development gave Rana something she had been fighting for all along: a little breathing room to keep her bus running.At 59, she is still showing upRana’s story is striking not simply because she is a woman working as a bus conductor at 59. It is because of the path that brought her there, from a daughter’s determination to fulfil her father’s dream, to taking on debt, surviving a pandemic-induced setback and eventually stepping onto the bus herself when the business needed her most. What began as an effort to honour her father's wish gradually became a journey of courage, resilience and determination. She does not appear to have set out to become a symbol of anything. She simply wanted to keep a promise. And every morning, when she climbs onto that bus and calls out the next stop, she is still keeping it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Florida teams have begun lowering 1,500 tons of repurposed concrete culverts into Gulf waters off Destin to create three artificial reefs; each 500-ton installation is intended to give marine life more shelter
articles.summary: A major marine construction project is underway off the coast of Okaloosa County, where workers have started placing three million pounds of recycled
articles.body: A major marine construction project is underway off the coast of Okaloosa County, where workers have started placing three million pounds of recycled concrete drainage pipes on the seabed to create three artificial reefs. The project involves lowering 1,500 tons of heavy concrete pipes into the Gulf of Mexico near Destin-Fort Walton Beach. Each of the three planned reef sites will receive around 500 tons of material. The pipes will be arranged in large groups to provide shelter and feeding areas for local marine life. According to information released by the Fish and Wildlife Foundation of Florida, the work is expected to continue through November 2026.Site selection and underwater structureThe concrete pipes are being placed at selected locations between four and eight nautical miles off East Pass. The water depth at the three sites ranges from 68 to 74 feet. Engineers have planned the arrangement of the heavy pipes to create complex underwater habitats on an otherwise flat, sandy seabed. Once the pipes settle on the ocean floor, their concrete surfaces will provide places for algae, barnacles and soft corals to grow and attach themselves. The hollow spaces inside the pipes will give smaller fish places to hide. The larger structures will also create hunting areas for bigger fish, including groupers, snappers and amberjacks. According to the Fish and Wildlife Foundation of Florida, the project aims to create more opportunities for both commercial and recreational fishing, as well as scuba diving in the region.Part of a broader state networkThe project near Destin-Fort Walton Beach is the second official reef placement under Florida's Coastal Corridor initiative. The statewide programme is jointly managed by the Fish and Wildlife Foundation of Florida and the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC). The first project under the initiative took place off the coast of Naples on 2 September 2026. By adding the Okaloosa County location, project managers are extending the conservation network into northwest Florida. The wider plan aims to connect marine habitats along both the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic coasts. These include natural coral reefs, artificial reefs, seagrass beds and coastal mangrove forests. “Three million pounds of reef material makes this a big deployment, but what excites us most is what it represents,” said Nick Wiley, Executive Director of the Fish and Wildlife Foundation of Florida, in an official statement. “We are beginning to turn the Coastal Corridor from a statewide vision into real habitat in Florida waters. Okaloosa County has been an outstanding partner, and this is exactly the kind of collaboration that will allow the initiative to grow from one community to the next.”Local partnerships and scientific planningLocal officials in Okaloosa County worked directly with state wildlife authorities to select the underwater locations. The county already manages several artificial reefs offshore, making it a suitable place to add more marine habitats. Okaloosa County Board Chairman Trey Goodwin welcomed the decision to bring state support and resources to local waters. “These collaborations are necessary to continue the statewide effort to improve habitat for marine life in the Gulf,” Goodwin said in public statements released by the foundation. “We appreciate the Fish and Wildlife Foundation of Florida for choosing Destin-Fort Walton Beach to add to our already vibrant artificial reef system.”State conservation officials said using strong materials such as heavy concrete pipes will help the new reefs survive powerful underwater currents and storm surges for many years. “Thoughtfully planned artificial reefs can play an important role in conserving and enhancing marine habitat while supporting the long-term health of Florida's fisheries,” said Roger Young, Executive Director of the FWC, in comments documented by the foundation. “Projects like this bring together sound science, careful site selection, durable materials, and strong local partnerships to create habitat that supports marine life and helps sustain healthy marine resources for generations to come.” As the placement work moves towards completion in late autumn, FWC scientists will monitor the new reefs. They will study how quickly fish begin to settle around the structures and how marine growth develops over time.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Vastu for Diwali Lights: Which Direction Should Your First Diya Face?
articles.summary: On Diwali evening, many homes have a small debate. Who lights the first diya? Where does it go? And which way should the flame face?
articles.body: On Diwali evening, many homes have a small debate. Who lights the first diya? Where does it go? And which way should the flame face? Most families follow whatever their grandparents did. Vastu Shastra, though, has fairly clear guidance. The direction a lamp’s wick points is believed to shape the blessings it invites. With Dhanteras on November 6 and Diwali on November 8, it’s worth getting the first lamp right.The Best Directions for the FlameEast. A diya with its wick facing east is linked to good health and long life. The east is the direction of the rising Sun, the source of vitality. Many families light their first lamp facing east in the puja room for exactly this reason.North. A wick facing north invites wealth and opportunity. The north belongs to Kubera, the treasurer of the gods, and is also linked with Goddess Lakshmi’s grace. On Lakshmi Puja night, a north-facing lamp near the locker, cash box or account books is considered especially auspicious.West. A west-facing wick is generally avoided in Vastu for regular lamps. It’s associated with sorrow and with energy moving away from the home.South. South is the direction of Yama, the god of death, so a south-facing flame is normally avoided. There’s one important exception. On the evening of Dhanteras, many families light a south-facing lamp outside the house as Yama deepdaan to protect the household from untimely death. That lamp is meant to face south.So for the first diya on Diwali, east or north is the right choice. If you’re unsure, east is the safest.Where the First Diya Should GoVastu places the first lamp in the home's most sacred spot, usually the puja room or the north-east corner. Placing it before the idol or picture of Lakshmi and Ganesha sets an auspicious tone for the evening.From there, many families light lamps outward. Next, they light a diya on each side of the main entrance to welcome Lakshmi. Then they light the tulsi plant, the kitchen, the area near the drinking water, and finally the balconies, windows, and rooftop.Traditionally, place a ghee lamp to the right of the deity and an oil lamp to the left. Ghee is linked to purity and divine blessings, while sesame or mustard oil is linked to protection and removing obstacles.Practical Tips for LightingClay diyas are preferred over plastic or metal for the main lamps. Clay comes from the earth and is believed to hold positive energy well. Brass or silver diyas are also fine for the puja room.Many households light diyas in odd numbers, such as five, seven, eleven or twenty-one. Odd numbers are considered auspicious in Hindu tradition.Keep lamps away from curtains and wooden furniture, and never leave them burning unattended in a room with small children or pets. Placing a diya on a small plate of rice or a metal stand prevents oil from spilling.Check that no lamp sits directly under a beam or inside a cluttered corner. Vastu treats clutter around a lamp as blocking the very energy it’s meant to invite.What About Electric Lights?Most homes now combine diyas with strings of electric lights. Vastu is more relaxed about these, but direction still matters a little. Warm white and yellow lights suit the east well. Green or blue tones fit the north. Red and orange shades suit the south-east, the direction of Agni, the fire element.Even with the brightest LED strings outside, the first lamp of Diwali should still be a real flame. That single diya, lit with intention and facing east or north, carries more meaning than any amount of decorative lighting.Get the latest astrology news and horoscope updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: In 2019, South Carolina sank a 95-foot retired tugboat 30 miles off Georgetown; it joined a deepwater reef known for snapper, grouper and other fish
articles.summary: In June 2019, South Carolina sunk a retired 95-foot tugboat named Susan Richards to create an artificial reef 30 miles offshore, boosting marine life habitats and recreational fishing opportunities.
articles.body: On June 28, 2019, a retired 95-foot tugboat named Susan Richards was intentionally sunk in the Atlantic Ocean off South Carolina. The Department of Natural Resources (SCDNR) deployed the vessel at Vermilion Reef, an artificial reef site approximately 30 miles offshore from Georgetown. On July 3, SCDNR announced the deployment while describing the tugboat as another addition to the state’s artificial reef programme.The transition from a working tugboat to an artificial reefThe Susan Richards had served a different purpose in the same coastal waters prior to its retirement. According to the department’s FY2019 annual report, the tugboat had towed numerous barge-loads of material to artificial reef sites along the South Carolina coast. This deployment transformed a vessel that was previously used in the construction of underwater habitats into an artificial reef structure itself.Due to unfavourable weather conditions, the sinking had been postponed for several weeks. Ultimately, on June 28, conditions were favourable enough for the operation to proceed. After deployment, the tugboat came to lie at approximately 120 feet underwater at artificial reef site PA-17, popularly known as Vermilion Reef. Though there are no physical surface buoys marking the location, the exact location of the site is published by the SCDNR for boaters, anglers and divers.Why South Carolina builds artificial reefsSand covers much of South Carolina’s continental shelf, thus leaving relatively little naturally occurring hard-bottom habitats where reef communities might develop. The department reported that only about 5 to 10% of the seafloor has the geological characteristics needed to support these communities. Natural hard-bottom areas provide surfaces where organisms like sponges, corals and other invertebrates can attach and grow. Suitable hard surfaces in otherwise sandy areas are added by artificial reefs, thus expanding the habitat available to marine life.These artificial structures, however, do not become mature reef communities immediately after submersion. Instead, over time their surfaces get colonised by algae, barnacles, sponges, corals, hydroids, bryozoans and marine worms. These organisms form the foundation of the developing reef community and contribute to its food web. Apart from this, crabs, shrimps, sea urchins and small fish may also gather around the structures for shelter and food. On the other hand, larger fish use these areas as breeding and feeding grounds.Examples of populations associated with South Carolina’s artificial reefs include red snapper, black sea bass, gag grouper and king mackerel. The 2019 SCDNR announcement shows that a range of fish species like grouper, jacks, triggerfish and Spanish hogfish are supported by the Vermilion Reef’s deeper offshore setting.Preparing retired vessels for deploymentArtificial reef material usually undergoes a cleaning process to ensure it is suitable for the environment before deployment. The state’s programme utilises different durable materials like steel and concrete structures, ships, tugboats, barges, military vehicles and subway cars.On the other hand, the Susan Richards project was funded through a partnership between SCDNR and the Coastal Conservation Association of South Carolina (CCA-SC). Additional support was provided from the revenue generated through saltwater fishing licence purchases. This particular placement was the programme’s ninth major artificial reef project completed in partnership with CCA-SC, thus reflecting the involvement of state conservation authorities and fishing organisations in expanding offshore habitat and recreational fishing opportunities.You use AI every day. articles.title: Uttarakhand chopper crash: Operation underway to recover bodies from  site
articles.summary: DEHRADUN: Rescue operations to recover the bodies of six people killed in a helicopter crash near Joshimath in Uttarakhand resumed at 5am on Saturday,
articles.body: DEHRADUN: Rescue operations to recover the bodies of six people killed in a helicopter crash near Joshimath in Uttarakhand resumed at 5am on Saturday, officials said. However, the difficult terrain and remote location are likely to make the operation challenging.The recovery work was stopped on Friday due to darkness and the presence of wild bears and other animals in the area.The privately operated helicopter, belonging to Trans Bharat Aviation, was carrying five pilgrims from Karnataka and a pilot when it crashed into a hillside in Joshimath. It was returning to Dehradun after ferrying pilgrims from the Badrinath shrine. All six people on board died in the crash.The bodies were located near the wreckage in Chai village. The district administration also sent a forest department team to the site on Saturday to assist with the recovery.A team from the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB), which is investigating the crash, was also expected to reach the site on Saturday.Speaking to the media, CM Pushkar Singh Dhami said an investigation had been ordered to establish the exact cause of the accident. He also expressed condolences to the families of the victims.Prateek Jain, chief executive officer of the Uttarakhand Civil Aviation Development Authority (UCADA), said the difficult terrain was making it challenging to recover the bodies. The remains would be carried on foot to Chamoli district headquarters and then taken to Dehradun after post-mortem examinations.On being asked about the decision to allow the helicopter to fly despite an India Meteorological Department (IMD) alert, Jain said an advisory had also been issued by the authorities. The circumstances surrounding the flight would now be examined as part of the investigation.Officials had said on Friday that the bodies would be taken to Joshimath for post-mortem examinations after recovery, with the process scheduled for Saturday.Meanwhile, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) said it had sent a team to Dehradun to carry out a preliminary assessment and regulatory review of the accident.Stay updated with the latest Dehradun news. articles.title: Glasgow’s historic Rogano restaurant failed to reopen after flooding and a fire as the UK Supreme Court rejected a claim for lost profits
articles.summary: Glasgow’s Rogano restaurant was unable to reopen after flooding and an electrical fire damaged its premises, prompting a legal dispute between its tenant
articles.body: Glasgow’s Rogano restaurant was unable to reopen after flooding and an electrical fire damaged its premises, prompting a legal dispute between its tenant and landlord. The case reached the UK Supreme Court after Forthwell Limited sought to recover profits lost by Lynnet Leisure (Rogano) Limited, the company that operated the restaurant.According to the UK Supreme Court (17 September 2026), the court dismissed Forthwell’s appeal over its claim for the subsidiary’s lost profits. It rejected the proposed legal exception under Scots law that would have allowed Forthwell to recover losses suffered by Lynnet. The court confirmed that the narrow Albazero exception remains part of Scots law, and left open whether the broader ‘performance interest’ ground applies. However, the appeal did not resolve the separate dispute over the landlord’s repair obligations.Court rejected Forthwell’s argument over lost restaurant profitsForthwell was the tenant of the Glasgow premises, while Pontegadea UK Limited was the landlord. Forthwell had allowed its wholly owned subsidiary, Lynnet Leisure (Rogano) Limited, to occupy the premises and operate the Rogano Restaurant and Bar. Lynnet was not a party to the lease. Forthwell argued it should be able to recover Lynnet’s lost profits and then account to Lynnet for them.The court rejected the legal exception Forthwell relied on and dismissed its appeal. It held that the proposed exception did not form part of Scots law.Flooding and fire damage sparked a dispute over RoganoThe Rogano had closed during the Covid-19 restrictions and could not reopen after its premises were damaged by flooding on 9 and 14 December 2020 and 10 January 2021. A fire broke out after the first flood, leaving the electrical installations unsafe. Water continued to enter the building, which was also left without heating.Forthwell argued that the landlord had failed to meet its obligations to repair the premises and maintain the building’s common areas. Under the lease, the landlord was required to rebuild any part damaged by an insured risk, including flooding. However, the two parties disagreed over the extent of the repairs needed and who was responsible for certain work. The repairs have not been carried out, and the restaurant has not been able to reopen.Lease dispute raised questions over lost restaurant profitsForthwell acquired the tenant’s interest in the lease in August 2013 and granted Lynnet a licence to occupy the premises. Lynnet operated the restaurant under that licence, but the lease was between Forthwell and Pontegadea legally. Forthwell sought an order requiring the landlord to carry out repairs or pay damages to cover their cost.Forthwell sought damages for Lynnet’s past and anticipated future lost profits. Pontegadea argued that Forthwell could not recover losses suffered by Lynnet because the subsidiary was not a party to the lease.Repair responsibilities remain unresolved after the court decisionThe Supreme Court held that the exception proposed by Forthwell was too broad and its limits were unclear. The general rule is that a party can recover damages for losses it has itself suffered, subject to exceptions. The court said the proposed approach could impose liability for losses involving a third party whose involvement was not contemplated when the contract was made.It also noted that existing legal routes may allow third parties to claim in some cases. The court found no convincing basis for creating the additional exception sought by Forthwell. It upheld the earlier decision rejecting the lost-profit claim.The parties told the court on the morning of the hearing that they had settled their dispute. Forthwell applied to withdraw its appeal, but the court refused, because the case raised a point of law of general public importance on which authoritative guidance was desirable. The separate questions about the landlord’s repair duties and the remedies sought were not determined by this appeal.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Wyoming woman wanted to keep her miniature goat as a pet; a dispute over a local livestock ban became a constitutional lawsuit
articles.summary: A Wyoming woman’s attempt to keep her miniature goat at home became a legal dispute over local animal regulations, the fairness of government decisions
articles.body: A Wyoming woman’s attempt to keep her miniature goat at home became a legal dispute over local animal regulations, the fairness of government decisions and constitutional rights. Venus Bontadelli, a resident of Powell, challenged the city’s permit process after officials refused to let her keep the animal as a pet. The disagreement raised questions about how local authorities classify companion animals and whether residents receive a fair opportunity to seek exceptions to restrictions. In January 2026, a settlement allowed the goat to return home, ending the immediate dispute without a court ruling on the constitutional claims.How did a Wyoming woman’s pet goat lead to a constitutional lawsuitThe case centred on Porsche Lane, a pygmy goat weighing about 20 pounds that had become part of the Bontadelli family. According to Wyoming Public Media, the goat was given to the family as a graduation present for their teenage daughter. She had been bottle-fed and raised as a companion animal.Bontadelli wanted to keep Porsche Lane at her home in Powell, but the city’s rules restricted livestock in residential areas. The family’s attempt to obtain permission through an exotic pet permit application became the starting point of the dispute.The Pacific Legal Foundation, which represented Bontadelli, argued that the city’s process was unfair. The organisation maintained that residents should have clear standards explaining when permission to keep an animal can be granted, rather than having applications depend on officials’ discretion.The disagreement was about more than whether a goat belonged in a residential neighbourhood. It also raised questions about how local governments make decisions affecting residents and whether their procedures provide adequate protection against arbitrary treatment.The city’s permit rules became the centre of the disputePacific Legal Foundation argued that the city’s approach made it difficult for residents to understand what they needed to demonstrate to receive approval.Local authorities can regulate animals in residential areas to address concerns such as public health, neighbourhood conditions and the potential problems associated with livestock. However, disputes can arise when a resident believes a regulation has been applied unfairly or when the process for obtaining an exception lacks clear requirements.Bontadelli viewed Porsche Lane as a household pet rather than an animal kept for agricultural purposes. The city’s restrictions created a conflict between that understanding and the rules governing which animals residents could keep.Cowboy State Daily reported that Bontadelli had sued Powell over the decision. Its coverage described her efforts to keep the goat and the legal challenge arising from the city’s restrictions.The dispute demonstrated how the classification of an animal can have practical consequences for its owner. Even a small goat raised for companionship may fall under rules intended to regulate livestock, leaving residents to seek permission from their local government.Why did the dispute raise constitutional concernsThe Pacific Legal Foundation filed the lawsuit in the US District Court for the District of Wyoming in November 2025. Its complaint argued that Powell’s ordinance violated the constitutional right to due process because the permit process did not provide sufficiently clear standards for deciding applications.Due process is a constitutional protection intended to ensure fairness in government procedures. In this case, the legal challenge focused on whether the city had established clear criteria governing who could receive permission to keep an otherwise restricted animal.The foundation argued that residents should not have to rely on uncertain or inconsistent decisions when seeking approval. Although cities have authority to establish rules for residential areas, those rules can be challenged when residents believe the procedures used to enforce them are constitutionally unfair.The lawsuit did not, however, result in a final judicial decision on those arguments. The case was resolved through a settlement before the court issued a ruling on the constitutional claims.What happened to Porsche Lane during the legal battleWhile the dispute continued, the family could not keep the goat at home. Wyoming Public Media reported that Porsche Lane had been sent to California to stay with a friend after the city refused permission for the animal to remain in Powell.The separation made the disagreement a personal matter for the family, which had raised the goat as a companion animal. Bontadelli’s case also attracted attention because it involved a relatively small pet rather than livestock kept for commercial purposes.According to the report, the city council rejected the family’s appeal. Concerns were also raised about whether allowing the application could lead to more residents keeping goats within city limits.A settlement allowed the goat to return homeIn a press release published on 14 January 2026, the Pacific Legal Foundation announced that Powell had agreed to issue Bontadelli a permit allowing Porsche Lane to return to the family. The settlement provided a practical resolution without requiring the court to decide whether the city’s rules were unconstitutional.The legal dispute had therefore achieved its immediate objective, although the settlement did not establish a general right for other Powell residents to keep miniature goats.You use AI every day. articles.title: A UN protection force must be urgently deployed to Palestine
articles.summary: Israel is making Palestinian existence in Palestine increasingly impossible.
articles.body:
For decades, the international response to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict has centred on the search for a political settlement.

Today, this strategy increasingly misses the more urgent issue: Palestinian civilian life and social structures are in grave danger because of the continuing colonisation of Palestine.

In Gaza, a genocidal war has killed more than 74,000 people and created the conditions for excess deaths of tens of thousands more. It has wiped out whole neighbourhoods, critical infrastructure and forced the education and healthcare systems into collapse.

In the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, different mechanisms of destruction operate: Settler and military violence, forced displacement, restrictions on movement, loss of access to agricultural land and livelihoods, fiscal pressure on Palestinian civil administration, etc.

Taken together, these policies affect the ability of Palestinian communities to continue to exist. For that reason, an international protection force is urgently needed not only to prevent Israeli violence, but to protect Palestinian schools, hospitals, access to livelihoods and access to aid.

The colonisation of Palestinian land has been going on for decades. Yet, since October 2023, it has accelerated to the point where Palestinian life in Palestine is made impossible.

Israel is not just killing Palestinians; it is actively destroying every pillar that supports human life: Housing, healthcare, education, livelihood, and security.

The Israeli army has destroyed roughly 81 percent of structures in Gaza, and left 1.9 million people displaced, without homes. The vast majority of the Strip’s residents live in tents or makeshift shelters that are unfit for long-term human habitation.

In the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, demolitions of homes, conducted under the pretext of absent building permits, have escalated. According to Al-Haq, 46 Palestinian communities were forcibly displaced by Israeli forces and settlers between 2023 and mid-2025. Other communities, including some in the heart of the West Bank, have been severely damaged, including the refugee camps of Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem. Most recently, Hebron has been besieged and homes there demolished; some 5,000 people have been displaced an at least 120 detained.

Heathcare and education are witnessing huge destruction. In Gaza, only 19 of 36 hospitals and only 73 of 158 primary health centres remain partially functional. According to UNICEF, 98 percent of Gaza’s schools were destroyed or damaged during the war.

In the occupied West Bank, hospitals are severely underfunded due to Israel withholding tax revenues from the Palestinian Authority (PA). As a result, they operate at reduced capacity, with a growing number of services becoming unavailable, while the hundreds of Israeli checkpoints prevent emergency care from functioning properly.

Education in the West Bank is also under threat. At least 84 schools, including in occupied East Jerusalem, remained under pending demolition or stop-work orders. Meanwhile, hundreds of thousands of children struggle with Israeli movement restrictions, which often render them unable to reach school.

Palestinian livelihoods have also been devastated. In Gaza, the carpet-bombing campaign has all but destroyed the economy, which was already crippled by the Israeli siege.

In the occupied West Bank, growing settler pogroms, land theft and designations of areas as “security zones” by the Israeli army have cut off Palestinian farmers from their land. Many have been unable to grow crops or harvest for three consecutive years, eliminating their primary income source.

While Palestinian agriculture is collapsing, the World Food Programme has announced it is cutting monthly food rations for hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank.

Employment opportunities have significantly shrunk. The Israeli authorities have withdrawn the work and travel permits that allowed Palestinians to work in Israeli enterprises.

While more than 90 percent of Palestinians in Gaza are without work, unemployment in the West Bank has doubled since 2023 by official counts, reaching 29.5 percent in 2026. This figure is likely an undercount, since workers unemployed for more than a year drop out of labour-force statistics.

Meanwhile, the PA, which is supposed to govern Palestinian life, has been transformed into Israel’s security subcontractor. As of 2026, Israel is withholding an estimated $4.8-5bn in tax and customs revenue collected on the PA’s behalf. It has, however, transferred enough money to ensure the PA’s security apparatus continues to function and actively engage in repression of the Palestinian people on its behalf.

All of this is happening against a backdrop of continuing colonial violence. In Gaza, the Israeli army bombs, shells and shoots at Palestinians daily. In the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers and soldiers kill, attack, burn and pillage.

If a population loses access to housing, cannot put food on the table, cannot receive healthcare or provide children with education, and faces constant violence, how can it survive? It cannot. And that is the reality Palestinians face today.

There is a clear legal basis for deploying a protective force in Palestine given that Israel is in violation of major pillars of international humanitarian law.

The International Court of Justice found that Israel’s occupation of Palestinian land is illegal and it needs to be brought to an end.

In a separate ruling, the ICJ held that Israel has an obligation to facilitate aid access into the Gaza Strip – access Israel has actively hindered.

Although advisory opinions are not binding, the fact that they place responsibility squarely on Israel as the occupying power provides a legal basis for demanding that this responsibility be enforced.

What compounds this is that Israel is not only the occupying power but also the party actively working to dismantle the collective civil life and nationhood of the Palestinian people.

So how can a protection force be constituted?

In the United Nations Charter, the Security Council is empowered to approve peace missions, but in the case of Palestine, that is effectively impossible, given the near-certainty of a US veto. A real alternative exists in the 1950 “Uniting for Peace” precedent, under which the General Assembly (UNGA) can recommend collective measures, including the use of force, when the Council is paralysed – a mechanism invoked roughly a dozen times since 1950, most recently on Ukraine in 2022.

Unlike a UNSC resolution, such a recommendation is not binding; its force is political rather than coercive. However, this could give legitimacy to a coalition of states who wish to take action and are willing to deploy and fund a protective force.

This coalition – plausibly including South Africa, which has already led the ICJ genocide case, alongside the Arab League and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation members – would need to bring this to the UNGA.

This route can be pursued while sustaining pressure on Washington, since durable protection ultimately requires removing US obstruction, not permanently routing around it.

The force that is ultimately deployed in Palestine should have a clear mandate to act on threats to Palestinian life. It should not replicate the Temporary International Presence in Hebron, which operated between 1994 and 2019 and was confined to observing and reporting abuses with no mandate to intervene.

The protective force must instead be mandated to keep Palestinians safe and establish a physical buffer between communities and settlers, with authority to prevent attacks rather than merely document them.

The deployment of such an international protection force must be the priority under the existing situation.

The protection of Palestinian society should be treated as an issue in its own right. Whatever the eventual political settlement, preserving the social, economic and cultural foundations of Palestinian civilian life cannot be deferred until a political settlement arrives.

articles.title: ‘Looks like Mars’: Toxic smog from Indonesia wildfires sparks health crisis, protests
articles.summary: Wildfires in Indonesia are blanketing the country and other southeast Asian nations in toxic smog, prompting widespread protests.
articles.body: Almost every day for months, Indonesian schoolteacher Natanael Undas has gazed up at smoke-filled skies in apocalyptic shades of yellow and orange. “It looks like Mars, like we’re living on another planet,” said Undas, whose home in central Kalimantan province is at the heart of devastating wildfires generating toxic smog in Indonesia and across Southeast Asia. Although his family keeps the windows shut at all times, the noxious smoke penetrates the house anyway, sending Undas’ 2-year-old daughter into constant sneezing fits amid a spike in respiratory illnesses in haze-affected regions. Wildfires are nothing new in Indonesia, whose forests and peatlands are set ablaze each year as family and commercial farms clear land using traditional “slash and burn” methods. But the fires this year are far worse than usual, said Undas, who has been documenting Indonesia’s air quality on Instagram since 2014, as heat and drought aggravated by a “super” El Niño weather pattern make this the country’s worst fire season in over a decade. The unrelenting haze from the fires has affected millions of people in the region since they started in July, closing schools in multiple countries and spurring arguments about who is to blame. Indonesian protesters have accused their government of insufficient action, while other countries are threatening prosecution. On Wednesday, hundreds of Indonesian students and members of civil society groups protested in the capital, Jakarta, and other cities against the policies of President Prabowo Subianto, including his resistance to declaring the fires a national disaster. “We want transparent and independent investigations about these wildfires,” protester Natasha Ruvantina told NBC News. “And also, we want a long-term prevention strategy.” The Indonesian government said in a statement Wednesday that it recognized the students’ concerns, adding that it was prosecuting companies linked to the fires and sending aid to affected provinces. The fires have also caused frustration in countries such as neighboring Singapore, where air pollution this month reached its highest level since 2015, when Indonesian wildfires were also intensified by El Niño. Singapore officials have threatened to prosecute companies seen as responsible for the devastation, and on Tuesday the foreign ministers of Singapore and Indonesia said they were considering a joint task force to combat illegal land burning. “We will use the full force of the law to make sure those who profit from fire must answer for the fires,” Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said. Indonesia’s neighbors and other countries have been accused of contributing to the problem. In a report this month, the Indonesian environmental organization Walhi named 66 companies with links to Singapore and 27 companies with links to Malaysia that it said were associated with fire hot spots. On Thursday, the Indonesian government said police had identified 20 corporations suspected of being involved in the fires, including four from Singapore, Malaysia and South Korea. The Malaysian government has denied that any Malaysian companies are involved, while the government of Singapore did not respond to a request for comment. Even as fingers are pointed across borders, the fires have been causing disruptions across the region, even threatening 67,000-year-old cave paintings on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi that are the oldest in the world. The haze also marred Singapore’s annual Formula One night race this month, obscuring the city’s iconic skyline during the globally watched event. “The biggest issue is a change in the quality of life,” Rajasekhar Balasubramanian, an engineering professor at the National University of Singapore, said of the haze. “People who usually participate in outdoor activities, for example, doing some kind of physical exercise, cannot do it anymore,” he said. A Singapore-focused study published in September found that short-term increases in airborne fine particulate matter were associated with increased emergency department visits for asthma and other chronic respiratory illnesses. According to the study, spikes in such visits in 2016 and 2019 coincided with periods of haze caused by Indonesian wildfires. In Indonesia, more than 283,000 cases of respiratory illness linked to the current fires had been reported in seven provinces as of Oct. 13, more than double the 113,000 cases reported as of Sept. 9, Reuters reported, citing Health Ministry data. Adeline Tong, a civil engineer in Singapore, said that the recent haze had brought back her long-dormant asthma and that if she goes outside without an N95 mask, “I will feel like I need my inhaler.” “Just two days ago, I could not even see the condo next to mine. It disappeared because the visibility was so bad,” she said in an interview on Oct. 21. While Tong is able to work remotely, she said the haze has affected her social life, discouraging her from meeting friends at the outdoor food courts and hawker stalls that are ubiquitous in Singapore. It has also affected her as a competitive ballroom dancer, she said. “I usually would run outside to train, but now I can’t do that because the outside air will make me feel worse and the gyms are so crowded now because no one is outside,” she said. For many others — including the scores of Indigenous tribes living in Borneo, an island divided among Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei where the fires are concentrated — staying indoors isn’t an option. Molly Wang and Marianna Madun are Penans, a seminomadic, hunter-gatherer tribe indigenous to Sarawak, a Malaysian state in Borneo near the fires in Kalimantan, the Indonesian part of the island. They live in a village of around 150 people in Sarawak’s Baram region, where they weave baskets and bags for a living. Wang said the fires and smoke had sent animals running deeper into the jungle, making it harder for the community to hunt, while Madun said gathering food had been difficult because the smoke irritates her eyes. The community has also paused traditional slash-and-burn farming techniques to avoid adding more smoke to the air. Wang said that while she doesn’t feel major health effects, older community members have been coughing and having trouble breathing; the closest clinic is an hour away by motorbike. Despite deploying thousands of personnel, Indonesia has struggled to quell the fires, which include vegetation fires above ground, as well as peat fires below. Peat fires “are very difficult to put out and continue to smolder for ages,” Balasubramanian said. “So when you have ripe, dry conditions, a small little incident could ignite wildfires above the surface, and it’s very hard to control.” Though the fires are expected to continue into early November because of a delayed rainy season, smaller showers this week have brought some relief, with firefighters in Indonesia dancing in delight and residents across the region celebrating the first “blue sky” days in weeks. “Finally, the rain comes,” Undas said.

articles.title: Hundreds from Russian-occupied Oleshky land in Belarus en route to Ukraine
articles.summary: Four planes transporting evacuees from the war-ravaged city have arrived in Belarus’s Gomel.
articles.body:
Hundreds of residents from the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky have been transported to Belarus, as part of a major evacuation mission under a truce that the White House says United States First Lady Melania Trump helped broker.

Four planes carrying the Oleshky evacuees arrived in the southeastern Belarusian town of Gomel on Saturday, said Ukrainian parliament member David Arakhamia.

The group was met in Gomel by rescue workers, medical teams and Red Cross volunteers, Belarusian state media reported.

From there, they were due to be transported to Ukrainian territory “within hours”, said Arakhamia.

The civilians from Oleshky, which has suffered from major food and medicine shortages after years of fighting, began the journey out of their region in bus convoys on Friday, under a rare regional truce that is expected to continue through Sunday.

The estimated 2,000 residents were offered the choice of travelling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but Melania Trump posted on Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.

Those travelling to Ukraine were first bused to the Russian city of Anapa, before being flown to Belarus.

“It was a very long journey for them,” Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said, reporting from Moscow.

“First more than a dozen buses took them to Anapa on the Black Sea… and then they spent several hours get to Gomel by plane”.

Shapovalova said the evacuees, including many children and elderly people, were waiting to head to the Novaya Guta checkpoint at the Ukraine-Belarus border.

Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from the Ukrainian side of the border where evacuees were expected to cross, said “a lot of preparation” was underway ahead of their arrival, with a large media presence and humanitarian aid workers on site.

“There’s food, there’s medical care, and, as we understand, this preparation has been going on for almost a week,” said MacAlpine.

Leonid Melinikov, a member of the Ukrainian Red Cross present at the border site, told Al Jazeera that aid workers were expecting around 500 arrivals.

Russia’s ombudswoman and lead representative on the evacuation mission, Yana Lantratova, said buses also transported Oleshky residents who wanted to live in Russia.

Those residents were first taken to a temporary accommodation centre in Simferopol in the Crimea region, said Shapovalova.

“We’re waiting for information on where and when they’re going to be taken next,” she said.

Aside from the first lady’s apparent role in the truce and evacuation mission, Pope Leo XIV – the first American pontiff – also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.

“The Russian military provided safe passage and safe corridors for the evacuees and were demining the roads near Oleshky,” said Shapovalova.

Moscow and Kyiv continued to trade attacks elsewhere even as the Oleshky truce continued.

The governor of Russia’s Bryansk region said a Ukrainian drone killed two people and injured five in the settlement of Klimovo on Saturday.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said overnight Russian attacks hit Ukrainian power plants, railway infrastructure and a gas distribution facility.

The strikes left more than 200,000 households without power in the Dnipro region, and 80,000 more without power in the Kyiv region, he said.

Zelenskyy, who has long pressed partners to supply Ukraine with more interceptors, renewed that call earlier on Saturday, saying: “Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day”.

While Zelenskyy welcomed the US approval of Kyiv’s purchase of 500 PAC-3 Patriot interceptors, he warned that equipment could take years to deliver and that Ukraine’s military needs the supplies more urgently.

“The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses,” said Zelenskyy in a post on X.

He urged allies to supply those existing interceptors immediately to cover Ukraine during the winter of 2026–2027, adding that partners could replenish their own stockpiles in subsequent years through the production already contracted and paid for.

articles.title: Europe braces for massive Halloween weekend protests over cost of living
articles.summary: Massive protests are set to take place across Europe on Saturday as part of demonstrations driven by the cost of living and deficient public services, with police braced for potential violence after recent looting and riots.
articles.body: Massive protests are set to take place across Europe on Saturday as part of demonstrations driven by the cost of living and deficient public services, with police braced for potential violence after recent looting and riots. Germany, France, Spain and Italy are among the nations expecting protests on Halloween following a recent wave of Gen-Z led marches across the continent. France will deploy a 70,000-strong police presence on Saturday, officials said, after some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education in the country evolved into wider demonstrations about the cost of living and social security. While the protests have been largely peaceful, police arrested 1,300 people last week after an estimated 410,000 took to the streets in cities across the country. Stores, public buildings and businesses have also been damaged since the protests erupted last month. “Everyone is ​on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told a news conference earlier this week as he set out security arrangements, adding there was “a very high ⁠risk” of unrest. Measures introduced last week to protect shops would be reinforced, and that demonstrations would not be permitted “in city centers, where there is a risk of public disorder,” he said. The United States Embassy in France has advised travelers to avoid areas ​where demonstrations or large gatherings are planned. The protests in France began after Prime Minister Emmanuel Macron launched budget talks for 2027. Students in the country angry over a declining education system and the high cost of living, then took to the streets. They were later joined by unions and the Yellow Vests, a grassroots movement that emerged in 2018 as a revolt against fuel taxes. Those demonstrations appear to have inspired similar protests across the continent, with protests erupting in Belgium, Spain, Italy and elsewhere. More than 160,000 people in Germany expected to join demonstrations organized by the campaign group Gen Z regelt (GenZ takes charge) in 34 cities on Saturday, including the capital Berlin and the financial hub Frankfurt. The groups demands spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and are against plans to return to mandatory military service. “We all have those images from France in our minds — looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers,” said Roman Poseck, interior minister for the state of Hesse, whose capital is Frankfurt. Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels. In the United Kingdom, hundreds of demonstrators are expected to risk arrest gather outside U.S. embassy in London on Saturday in support of Palestine Action, a protest group banned by the British government. In Serbia, student-led activism also helped unseat the country’s long-time leader at the ballot box. In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year after groups of masked protesters looted stores in the fashion capital and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police earlier this month. Tens of thousands of people again took to the streets of Rome on Friday and other cities and towns across the country. The demonstrations were largely peaceful but an NBC News crew saw police use a water cannon on protesters and groups of police charging to disperse protesters. Italian police were out in force with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the capital. “We have been completely screwed by the fact that the wages do not keep up on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the cost of living,” said Luca, a 20-year-old medical student who asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.
