articles.title: It’s the world’s largest passenger plane. But he still fit some of it inside his home
articles.summary: In our roundup of travel stories this week: aviation’s strangest four-engine giant passenger plane, the luxury 1980s private jet you can book for a private stay, plus the A380 superfan who has outfitted his home like a first-class cabin.
articles.body: In our roundup of travel stories this week: Aviation’s strangest four-engine giant passenger plane, the luxury 1980s private jet you can book for a private stay, plus the A380 superfan who has outfitted his home like a first-class cabin. In love with a superjumbo It wasn’t love at first flight for aviation superfan Arun Rajagopal and the Airbus A380. The turning point came on his fourth journey aboard the world’s largest passenger plane, flying business class to Singapore. “The seats were huge, and you have a bar in the back of the plane,” he said. It gave him a “wow” feeling, like “experiencing comfort on another level.” Soon, he was flying A380s as often as possible. So far he’s clocked 220 times and counting, covering roughly 715,000 miles across six continents. In recent years, he’s brought the A380 experience into his own Dubai apartment as well. He has two first-class seats from Emirates’ first A380, first-class cabin lamps, and an A380 wheel upcycled into a coffee table. The pièce de résistance, however, is the meticulously restored and customized living-room from The Residence – Etihad Airways’ luxurious three-room private suite – which he spent a year constructing in his living room. See more of his A380 treasures here. The commercial flop that won hearts The Airbus A340-600 broke records as the world’s longest passenger plane when it was launched in 2002, but for most of the decades it’s been flying, it’s been a commercial flop. Its four engines are thirsty and its 247-foot-long fuselage requires special runway clearance. On top of this, its quirky design includes a downstairs lavatory tucked away in space usually reserved for cargo – which apparently has made it a tempting proposition for would-be members of the Mile-High Club. While it never was a hit with the airline industry, the Airbus A340-600 has a strong cult following among aviation fans and aircrews, many of whom turned out at Washington Dulles International Airport this month to see the arrival of a flight that would mark the end of German carrier Lufthansa’s relationship with the aircraft. Auf wiedersehen, jet (subscribers only). Low-cost private jet experience For an in-the-clouds experience at very grounded prices, vacationers in Bristol, England, can stay in a vintage Boeing 727 with a luxury 1980s retro interior. Known as PytchAir, the retired airliner has been converted into a 1,000-square-foot, fully micro-grid-powered stay by local entrepreneur Johnny Palmer. Resting atop a stack of shipping containers and generating more solar and wind energy than it actually uses, the property offers aviation enthusiasts full access to a Miami Vice-era time capsule, complete with two lounges, a main bedroom and an open flight deck where guests can push every button in sight. Despite the excessive 1980s opulence of its interior, it is unlikely, as rumors have it, that it ever belonged to Colombian drug lord Pablo Escobar. In 2013, Anthony Bourdain visited Colombia for his series “Parts Unknown,” to see how the country was recovering from the stereotypes of earlier decades. CNN subscribers can watch here. Endless cruise comes to an end The cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey, which has been sailing around the world continuously for more than two years in what its residents hoped was a “forever” cruise, has abruptly halted operations. Passengers were evicted in Cambodia after the company Villa Vie Residences said the Iran war made fuel prices too expensive to continue its voyage In case you missed it Sadly, it’s not just cruise companies affected by higher fuel costs. Airfares are expected to soar this holiday season. It’s nearly 90 years since aviator Amelia Earhart disappeared. Our interactive story follows the enduring quest. She set off traveling alone at age 13. And now she’s visited nearly every country. (Subscribers only.) A campaign revelation. A cancelled cruise. A baseball showdown. What do you remember from the week that was?

articles.title: Cost-of-living protests set to spread to Germany on Halloween as France braces for fresh unrest
articles.summary: Cost-of-living protests that began in France are spreading to Germany with hundreds of thousands of people expected to turn out in cities across the country on Saturday that coincide with Halloween.
articles.body: Cost-of-living protests that began in France are spreading to Germany with tens of thousands of people expected to turn out across the country on Saturday for demonstrations that coincide with Halloween. The new German youth-led movement dubbed “Gen Z has got this!” will see people protest against the high cost of living, underfunded schools and universities, environmental concerns and a potential reintroduction of mandatory military service. Protests are planned in major cities including Berlin, Frankfurt, Cologne and Munich. Organizers of ‘Gen Z regelt’ planned the large day of action to coincide with Halloween, to maximize turnout and visibility. “We are young people who no longer want to watch decisions being made about our future without us,” the movement states on its website. It adds that the intention is to protest peacefully and organizers instruct participants to keep their faces visible, even in Halloween costumes. Extra German police officers have been deployed nationwide in preparation for the protest, and the luxury shops lining Berlin’s upmarket Kurfürstendamm shopping street have boarded up their windows as a precautionary measure. The German youth movement follows a broader wave of protests that have swept Europe, including significant unrest in France, which has been hit by rioting and looting and is now facing another weekend of rallies. The Yellow Vests movement has called for nationwide protests on Saturday, billed as the third act of demonstrations, following earlier protests on October 17 and 24. Students and some unions are also expected to join. Warning of a “very high risk of public disorder,” France’s Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez announced this week that demonstrations would only be authorized outside town centers, with 70,000 extra law enforcement officers deployed nationwide. Halloween is adding a new complication to the protests, with Nuñez warning of separate calls for gatherings across France from 8 p.m. local time “by radical far-left groups and radicalized Yellow Vests.” He said some messages invoked Halloween while calling for “revolution” and “insurrection”, describing them as incitements to serious public disorder and warning that the gatherings would be banned. In recent days, the word “purge” has been circulating across social media platforms, a reference to the dystopian film franchise which depicts a world where all crime is legalized for a 12-hour period each year. “At Halloween, the rules remain the same!” warned the Paris police on X, reminding people that concealing one’s face in public is punishable by a €150 ($170) fine, while carrying a weapon, even a fake one, can carry a sentence of up to three years in prison and a €45,000 fine. The French protests began in late September, led by high school students demanding improvements to deteriorating school buildings, teacher shortages and a lack of resources, as well as changes to the university admissions system. France saw yet another wave of protests this weekend, with some 70,000 officers positioned across the country to prevent a repeat of the kind of violence and riots that hit the nation last week.Demonstrations remained largely peaceful today, but some cities saw clashes, with police deploying water cannon and tear gas. At least 400,000 people protested across France, 110,000 of these in Paris, the interior ministry said. At least 1,000 people were detained, authorities said.Last week’s violence followed weeks of protests over education, dismal job prospects and the cost of living. Initially peaceful and attended mostly by students, the demonstrations quickly turned into the worst wave of deadly, nationwide violence in years.Police fired tear gas into crowds and fought running battles with black-clad, hooded rioters who set fires and broke into thousands of shops and government buildings. More than 2,000 people were arrested, with at least two deaths and reports of serious injuries.This week, curfews were imposed in some cities to help maintain calm. Some 70,000 police officers will be have been deployed across the country over the weekend, according to the interior ministry. Specialist SWAT units, helicopters, armored vehicles, police dogs and water cannons will all be part of the operation. The protests then morphed into something bigger, with the Yellow Vests – which began as a movement against soaring fuel prices – among those taking to the streets. The images of violence and looting from the October 17 protests are still haunting French officials. That day, more than 550,000 people took to the streets across France, according to the Interior Ministry more than 3,000 shops were attacked or looted, with some destroyed and over 2,700 people were arrested. The interior minister said more than 1,000 law enforcement officers have been injured since the beginning of the protest movement. Asked about the students injured during the protests, President Emmanuel Macron described the violence as a “collective failure”. “I think no high school student started pushing for their demands expecting to suffer such terrible consequences. And I don’t know a single police officer who signed up to find themselves caught up in such terrible and violent moments either,” he told Youtuber Hugo Travers. Saturday’s demonstration comes ahead of November 5, when all eyes will be on a nationwide strike and mobilization called by the inter-union coalition over rising living costs.
